items.stem: What does the checks-effects-interactions pattern protect against?

options.text: Reentrancy, by updating state before making external calls
options.rationale: Correct: updating state first prevents a called contract from re-entering with stale state.
That is a separate concern (SafeMath/0.8 checks).
It is a security pattern, not a gas optimisation.
It does not address compile errors.

items.stem: Why is relying on tx.origin for authorization in Solidity dangerous?

options.text: A malicious intermediary contract can trick a user into calling it, passing the origin check
options.rationale: Correct: tx.origin enables phishing-style attacks; use msg.sender instead.
It is not zero; it is the original sender.
Gas is unrelated to this risk.

options.text: tx.origin cannot be read in a contract
options.rationale: It can be read, which is the problem.

items.explanation: Correct: tx.origin enables phishing-style attacks; use msg.sender instead.

items.stem: Which statements about Solidity smart contracts are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Deployed contract code is immutable unless an upgrade pattern was designed in
options.rationale: Correct: you cannot simply edit deployed bytecode.

options.text: The pull/withdrawal pattern is safer than pushing Ether to many recipients
options.rationale: Correct: it avoids failures and reentrancy from external pushes.

options.text: State variables live in memory and vanish after each call
options.rationale: False; state lives in persistent storage.

options.text: Functions are private by default, so visibility never matters
options.rationale: False; explicit visibility is required and important.

items.explanation: Correct: you cannot simply edit deployed bytecode.; Correct: it avoids failures and reentrancy from external pushes.
